# The Value of Disagreement

## Why a Good Meeting Doesn't End in Consensus

There's a common assumption, baked into how most of us were taught to work, that a successful meeting is one where everyone walks out nodding. The goal, we implicitly believe, is alignment—heads around the table, a shared plan, a chorus of agreement. And when a meeting ends with people still arguing, we tend to feel it failed. Something went wrong. Someone wasn't persuasive enough, or someone else was being difficult.

But this instinct deserves a second look. Agreement, it turns out, is often a poor measure of progress. Sometimes it reflects genuine shared understanding. But it can also conceal confusion, unspoken doubt, fatigue, or the quiet desire to just get out of the room. People say "sure, that works" for many reasons, and only one of them is that they actually believe it works. A meeting that ends in harmony may have simply succeeded in hiding the disagreement rather than resolving it.

The alternative is stranger and more demanding: a good meeting can end with a precise, honest map of what people disagree about.
